Roles explained

Planner, coordinator or stylist: which one do you need?

Three different jobs, three different fees, and three different things that turn up on the day. Almost every confusing planning quote in Australia comes from asking for one of them and describing another.

Get event planning quotesSee what each one costs
  • Written for Australian events
  • No jargon
  • Updated September 2026

What does an event planner do?

An event planner builds the plan. From a brief, a date and a budget, they develop the concept, shortlist and secure the venue, source and book every supplier, hold the budget, build the timeline, and then manage the event itself. The work is spread over months and the majority of it happens long before anyone sees a table setting.

The part people underestimate is the sequencing. A planner knows which decisions have to be made first because they constrain the others, and which can safely wait. That is why a planner engaged in month one is worth more than the same planner engaged in month nine, even though the visible output looks similar.

The part people overestimate is the taste. A planner is not there to tell you what your event should look like. They are there to make your version of it happen on time and inside budget, and to tell you honestly when something will not work.

What does a coordinator do?

A coordinator runs a plan that already exists. They arrive near the end, typically four to six weeks out, take everything you have built, confirm every supplier, write the run sheet that all of them work from, and manage the event on the day from bump in through to pack down.

A coordinator does not choose your suppliers, negotiate your contracts or build your budget. They are not being paid to have opinions about your florist. They are being paid to make sure the florist arrives at the right time, through the right door, with enough time to install before guests walk in.

Coordination is the most commonly bought planning product in Australia, and the reason is simple. Most people can hold a plan together for months. Almost nobody can host an event and run it at the same time.

What does a stylist do, and why is it a different search?

A stylist designs how the event looks and supplies or specifies the physical things that make it look that way: the furniture, the linen, the backdrops, the signage, the tablescape and the installation. It is a design and supply job, not a management job.

A stylist will not chase your celebrant, reconcile your budget or write your run sheet, and a planner will not usually turn up with a truck of hire furniture. Where the two meet is that a planner sets the styling direction and then engages a stylist or a hire company to deliver it.

This matters practically. If what you actually want is a beautiful room and you already have the logistics under control, you are looking for a stylist or an event hire company, and Plan Your Event is the wrong starting point. If what you want is someone to run the whole thing, keep reading.

Why the titles blur

Why does everyone use these words differently?

Because the titles are not regulated and most Australian businesses sell more than one of them. A single business might offer full planning, partial planning, on-the-day coordination and styling, and describe itself on its homepage as a wedding planner. That is not misleading. It just means the title tells you about the business, not about the product you are buying.

So stop reading the title and read the inclusions. The three questions that resolve almost every case are: who books the suppliers, who holds the budget, and when does the person start. Those three answers place any quote you receive on the table above, whatever the business calls itself.

Getting it wrong

What happens when you hire the wrong one

None of these are hypothetical. They are the four mismatches that produce the awkward conversations, and each one has a tell you can spot before you sign.

You hired a coordinator but needed a planner

The tell is that you are still choosing suppliers in month two of a six week engagement. A coordinator will help where they can, but they were quoted to confirm bookings, not to make them, and the timeline they inherited has holes in it. The fix costs money because the scope has to be renegotiated mid-engagement.

You hired a planner but only needed a coordinator

The tell is that the venue, the photographer, the celebrant and the caterer were all booked before you engaged anyone. You are paying full planning rates for a job that is mostly confirmation. A good planner will tell you this in the first call and quote you down. Not all of them do.

You hired a stylist and expected management

The tell is that nobody has asked you for supplier contact details. A stylist is designing and installing, and will leave once the install is done. On the day, the run sheet, the supplier calls and the problems are still yours.

You relied on the venue coordinator for everything

The tell is a ceremony at a different site, or three suppliers who are not in the venue contract. The venue coordinator is excellent inside the building and has no authority or responsibility outside it, which is most of a wedding day.

The fourth title

What a venue coordinator does, and does not

A venue coordinator is employed by your venue. Their job is to make the venue run properly on the day: the room set-up, the catering service, the floor staff, the bar, the venue's own timings and the venue's own rules. On most Australian packaged venues they are included in the venue fee, which is why so many couples assume they do not need anyone else.

What they do not do is work for you. They will not source your photographer, chase your celebrant, reconcile your budget across twelve suppliers, or tell you that your 4pm ceremony will not leave enough light. They are usually not on site for a ceremony held somewhere else, they generally finish when the venue's service does, and they may be running two functions that day.

Ask your venue three questions in writing. Will the same person be there on the day, or is the role covered by whoever is rostered? What time do they start and finish? And are they responsible for suppliers who are not part of the venue contract? The answers tell you immediately whether you also need a coordinator of your own.

Deciding

Which one do you need?

Four questions. Answer them honestly and the choice is usually obvious.

01

Have you booked the venue?

If no, you want a planner. The venue constrains capacity, catering, bump in and often the supplier list, so almost every other decision waits on it.

02

How many suppliers will you manage?

Under about five at a venue that handles catering and staffing, coordination is usually enough. Over about ten, or at a dry hire site, planning starts doing real work.

03

Is the problem the decisions or the day?

If the plan has stalled and you cannot face the choices, that is partial planning. If the plan is fine and the day is the worry, that is coordination.

04

Is the problem how it looks?

If the logistics are handled and what you want is the room to look a particular way, you are looking for a stylist or an event hire company rather than a planner.

Your side

What each role needs from you

The three roles fail for different reasons, and in each case the failure usually starts with something the client did not supply.

A planner needs a decision-maker

One person who can say yes. Planning stalls fastest when every choice has to go back to a committee of four, because the supplier holding the date will not wait a fortnight for an answer. Nominate the person who decides, and tell the planner who it is.

A planner needs the real budget

Not the aspirational one. A planner who is given a number twenty per cent above what you can actually spend will build a plan you have to dismantle in month six, and dismantling costs more than building carefully.

See the cost guide

A coordinator needs your paperwork

Every supplier contract, every contact name and mobile, the floor plan, your timings, the seating chart and the access restrictions. A coordinator handed a folder that is missing three contracts spends the handover chasing documents instead of finding conflicts.

How the handover works

A coordinator needs your worries

The honest list of what you think might go wrong. The uncle who will speak for twenty minutes, the supplier who has gone quiet, the family seating problem. This is the single most useful thing you can hand over and the thing people most often leave out.

A stylist needs constraints, not just images

A mood board without the venue's restrictions, the budget and the dimensions produces a design you cannot install. Give them what cannot change before you give them what you like.

Timing

When to hire a wedding planner

For full wedding planning in Australia, nine to fourteen months before the date is the normal window, and twelve to eighteen months is better if your date is a Saturday in March, April, October or November. Planners take a limited number of weddings per season, and the peak Saturdays go first.

Partial planning usually begins four to eight months out, which is when most couples discover that the venue was the easy part. On-the-day coordination is typically booked two to three months out so the handover can start four to six weeks before the wedding. Inside six weeks, some coordinators will decline, not to be difficult but because they cannot do the supplier confirmation work properly in the time left.

There is no penalty for enquiring early. Enquiring costs nothing, and the main thing it buys you is choice, because you are comparing planners who are still free rather than the ones who happen to be left.

The conversation

Questions to ask a wedding planner before you sign

Ten questions that separate a good fit from an expensive one. The last three matter most and almost nobody asks them.

Which level am I buying, in writing?

Full, partial or coordination, with the inclusion list attached to the contract. Ask what happens to the fee if the scope changes in month four.

How many events do you take in a season?

A planner running eight weddings a month is a different proposition from one running two. Neither is wrong. You want to know which you are hiring.

Who will actually be at my event?

Some planners run every event personally. Others send a team coordinator. Ask to meet the person who will be on site.

What is excluded?

Travel outside a radius, extra site visits, meetings past a set number, styling hire and additional on-site staff are the usual five.

How do you charge, and on what?

Flat fee or percentage. If percentage, ask what it is calculated on and whether there is a floor.

See the cost guide

How often will I hear from you?

A defined communication rhythm prevents the most common complaint about planners, which is silence in the middle months.

Have you worked at my venue?

Or at venues like it. A planner who has done a bump in at your site already knows its restrictions.

What happens if a supplier fails?

Every experienced planner has this story. The answer tells you how they think under pressure and whether they have a backup network.

What does the contract say about cancellation?

Deposit, payment schedule, postponement and cancellation. Read it before you sign, not after something changes.

What would you push back on in my plan?

The most useful question on the list. A planner who has no reservations about a plan they have just heard for the first time is not paying attention.

Straight answers

Role questions, answered

What does an event planner do?

An event planner builds and runs the plan behind an event: the concept, the venue, the supplier sourcing and booking, the contracts, the budget, the timeline and the management of the day. How much of that list applies depends on whether you buy full planning, partial planning or coordination only.

Is a coordinator cheaper than a planner?

Usually, because it is a smaller product rather than a cheaper person. Published Australian figures put day-of coordination at roughly $1,500 to $2,000 (Easy Weddings, February 2026) against $5,000 to $6,000 for full-service planning. You are buying six weeks of work instead of nine months of it.

Do I need both a planner and a coordinator?

Rarely. A full planning package normally includes running the day, so you would be paying twice. The exception is where a planner hands over to a dedicated on-site coordinator from the same business for a large event, which should be inside one fee rather than two.

Can one person be a planner and a stylist?

Yes, and many Australian businesses offer both. Ask for the two scopes quoted separately so you can see what you are paying for each, and so you can compare the styling scope against a dedicated stylist or hire company if you want to.

When should I hire a wedding planner?

Nine to fourteen months out for full planning, four to eight months out for partial planning, and two to three months out for on-the-day coordination. Bring all of those forward if your date is a Saturday in the March to April or October to November peak.

What is the difference between a wedding coordinator and a venue coordinator?

A venue coordinator works for the venue and manages what happens inside it, usually included in your venue fee. A wedding coordinator works for you and manages your whole day, including the suppliers outside the venue contract and the ceremony if it is elsewhere. Many couples have both. Our wedding coordinators page sets the two out side by side.
